title: Two intrinsic differences: residual principle of repair; eternal vs temporal debt
source_text: XXIII. Unde colligunt peccatum veniale, ex se & natura sua, a peccato mortali dupliciter differre. Primum in eo quod peccatum mortale, cum vitam animae extinguat, & Dei gratiam ex anima expellat, nullum in homine principium relinquit, cujus vi tolli & deleri queat: sed ad hoc opus est ut Deus de novo quasi hominem ex mortuis excitet. Cum res secus se habeat in peccato veniali, sicuti jam dictum est. Deinde in eo quod, si cogitemus peccatum mortale retractatum fuisse per aliquem actum contritionis & dilectionis, & ita ex anima sublatum, quoad pravitatem, & maculam ex eo relictam: at nihilominus Deum de jure suo, & poena quam exigere potest, nihil homini remittere velle, qui peccatum tale admisit ad poenam aeternam obligatus manet; propter legem Dei semel per illud violatam. Cum sublata culpa peccati venialis, nullum poenae aeternae debitum in homine manere possit, sed solummodo debitum poenae cujusdam temporalis. Quae est Bellarmini doctrina, De Amissione Gratiae, lib. 1. cap. 13. Responsione ad 3. Objectionem.
pass_a_gloss: Whence they gather that venial sin, of itself and by its own nature, differs from mortal sin in a twofold way. First in this, that mortal sin, since it extinguishes the life of the soul and drives God’s grace out of the soul, leaves in the person no principle by whose force it can be taken away and blotted out: but for this it is needful that God as it were raise the person anew from the dead. Whereas the matter stands otherwise in venial sin, as has already been said. Next in this, that if we should think mortal sin to have been retracted by some act of contrition and love, and so taken away from the soul as to the wickedness and the stain left from it—yet God still unwilling to remit anything of His right and of the punishment He can exact—he who admitted such a sin remains bound to eternal punishment, because of God’s law once violated through it. Whereas when the guilt of venial sin is taken away, no debt of eternal punishment can remain in the person, but only the debt of a certain temporal punishment. Which is Bellarmine’s doctrine, On the Loss of Grace, book 1, chapter 13, Reply to the third Objection.
pass_b_english: Mortal sin leaves no inward principle of repair—God must raise as from the dead; venial leaves grace’s life intact.
Even after contrition, unpaid mortal debt can still be eternal; cleared venial guilt leaves only temporal dues—Bellarmine’s line.

choices.why: Grace as spiritual life extinguished by mortal sin.
